newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Walesa says Russians won't block Poland's NATO entry.
newsitem.headline: Walesa says Russians won't block Poland's NATO entry.

text.p: Former Polish leader Lech Walesa said in an interview published on Sunday that no Russian leader would risk using force to prevent Poland entering NATO.

Asked by Argentine newspaper La Nacion in Warsaw whether Poland's entrance to the Western alliance would be at risk if President Boris Yeltsin were replaced by another Russian leader, Walesea replied, "No one in Moscow who knows how to calculate will take such a risk...Neither Poland nor NATO want to invade Russia and the Russians know it. Russia isn't in any condition to invade anyone either."
Walesa said that Russian opposition to the entrance of former Eastern bloc countries to NATO was due to lack of democratic experience and would turn out to be composed of idle threats.

"They have lost their ideology, they haven'd found a new one, and, without democratic experience, they are looking for a threat as an incentive to act," he said, "But I think that that's just propaganda for the moment."

Walesa said that he thought Eastern European countries should join NATO not because they can realistically expect to be defended in case of war, but rather because it cements them firmly into a peaceful group of allied nations.

"No one is going to start a nuclear war because of Poland. I want to enter NATO in the peaceful sense. It's very easy: one block grows and so there isn't anything left to form another block...And so we have peace," he said.
The Russians will probably become closer to the West once their economy starts to grow, Walesa said.

"What will happen in Russia manages to improve its economy? The Russians are going to like to be able to visit Washington, Paris, London, New York. There are times when it is worth ending the pattern of confrontation."
A former union boss and 1983 Nobel Peace Prize winner who became Poland's first post-communist leader in 1990, Walesa said that he was in a sense satisfied to have lost elections in 1995.

"In democracy, the people who are best organised, with the best organisation, and have the most money are the ones who win. In revolutions the one who shows that he is a leader, not the political parties, is the one who wins...If I had won, that would have meant that the revolution was continuing and that, in a way, I had failed in my struggle. The world and the Poles should be glad of that."
